title: Sophocles, Hesiod, Euripides (18 tragedies), and Aeschylus
shelf_note: A Byzantine minuscule manuscript of the tragedians (Laurenziana); the sampled pages are Sophocles' Electra, Euripides' Bacchae and Medea. Squarely on a Greek classics shelf.
structure_note: printed_repeats 143 / backsteps 33 fit a leaf-foliated manuscript (a modern folio number on rectos only: '80' on p173, '175' on p363, with versos unnumbered), not a defect. pages_translated counted 503 against a stored 472. p524 is a blank back endleaf, correctly marked blank.

reader_summary: A 14th-century-style Byzantine manuscript of Sophocles, Euripides and others, with interlinear glosses. The images are good, but the transcription of the text pages is mostly made up: it keeps a few real lines and fills the rest with plausible Greek, labels Electra's lyric exchange as a scene with Orestes, and duplicates every line as a gloss. The English is a fluent translation of that invented text and cannot be trusted.
book_verdict: Good images, unusable text: three of three text pages are largely confabulated OCR with confident English on top, plus markup leaking into the reader.

reader_summary: Proclus' commentary on Plato's Alcibiades in a clear humanist Greek hand. The transcription follows the right text and most words are right, but every sampled page has misreadings that change the sense: the Phaedo becomes 'potentiality', physicians become singers, and on one page a 'therefore' becomes a 'not', so the English says the opposite of Proclus. A scholar would need Westerink's edition beside it.
book_verdict: Right text, readable images, but meaning-changing misreadings on 4 of 4 pages, one reversed sentence, and markup leaking into the reader; not fit to show without correction.

title: Quaestiones de Primis Principiis
shelf_note: Kopp's 1826 edition of Damascius' Problems and Solutions concerning First Principles: Greek text with Latin critical notes. A core late-Neoplatonist text.
structure_note: Catalogue language says 'Latin', but the body text is Greek; only the footnotes are Latin (I7). The 1826 Frankfurt edition is public domain (Google scan). The 14 backsteps / 10 repeats are probably misread printed page numbers on a cleanly paginated book; the sampled pages carry correct numbers (82, 111, 216, 342).

reader_summary: Kopp's 1826 edition of Damascius on first principles, with the Greek transcribed almost perfectly, footnotes included. The English is a careful, literal rendering of the Greek that a reader can follow, with occasional dropped opening clauses and one or two muddled sentences; Kopp's Latin notes are not translated.
book_verdict: Excellent transcription and a mostly faithful translation; warn about silently dropped clauses at page starts and the untranslated Latin apparatus, and fix the catalogue language (Greek, not Latin).

title: Vitruvii de architectura libri X
shelf_note: A medieval (12th–13th-century) Laurenziana copy of Vitruvius, De architectura; it belongs here.
structure_note: Folio numbers are written top-left on rectos ('54.' on p60), so with_printed_number 84/116 and the backsteps are most likely folio numbers misread from flyleaves and versos rather than a splice. p115 is a back flyleaf with marginal inscriptions in Arabic script. The OCR convention flips between pages: p24 and p60 are kept abbreviated (diplomatic), while p30 is expanded and normalised.

reader_summary: A medieval manuscript copy of Vitruvius' On Architecture, with clean images of a dense abbreviated hand. The transcription is the right text but uneven: one page is close, another is partly invented (Socrates becomes a 'father-in-law', whole sentences replaced), and the English drops half of one page and speaks of 'Indians' where Vitruvius says southern peoples. Not reliable for citation.
book_verdict: Right work and good images, but invented OCR on one page, a half-page omission in translation on another, and named-entity errors that change what Vitruvius says.
